newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian tax police raid Almazy Rossii-Sakha.
newsitem.headline: Russian tax police raid Almazy Rossii-Sakha.

text.p: Russian tax police have raided the Moscow and Siberian head offices of the Almazy Rossii-Sakha diamond producer and confiscated documents, ARS spokesman Valentin Logunov said on Friday.
"They conducted this operation yesterday (Thursday)," he said, adding, "It's my impression that with the tax police working, the agreement with De Beers will again be dragged out."
ARS is Russia's sole authorised gem producer and De Beers' partner.
De Beers controls about three quarters of the world diamond market, and Russia, through ARS, accounts for about 25 percent of all the rough gems De Beers sells.
Logunov said the raid took place "in an orderly fashion" but that ARS was not eager to publicise the event.
"We didn't want to attract attention to this," he said. "It was of course highly undesirable as well as unpleasant."
He stressed that he was expressing his own opinion about the effect of the raid on the stalled De Beers deal, saying that ARS had not issued a formal statement on the matter.
The operation took place at ARS offices in Moscow and in far-flung Mirny, in Siberia. "They've occupied the whole company," Logunov said.
He said unnamed people were working to split ARS into separate mining and export companies with the aim of gaining the upper hand over Russia's lucrative rough diamond exports.
Russia's prosecutor-general's office said in November 1996 that it was investigating ARS finances.
The tax raid is the latest concern for De Beers in its troubled relationship with Russia.
De Beers made good on a promise to stop all purchases of Russian diamonds on December 31, 1996 when it cancelled its interim trade scheme after Moscow failed to approve or reject a new trade deal.
A new draft deal requires signatures by recuperating President Boris Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, but De Beers officials do not know when a deal might be signed.
ARS production was worth $1.38 billion in 1996. Under previous deals, the company sold around 95 percent of its rough diamonds to De Beers.
